engine: offline illustrative deterministic protocol models, not real network behavior

cases.q: A client times out after its HTTP handler has committed an order. Which layer distinguishes a transport timeout from a rejected order?
cases.setup: Synthetic pipeline: DNS=6 ms, TCP=11 ms, TLS=14 ms, application=27 ms, response transfer=3 ms; no assumed concurrency.
cases.derive: The sequential trace totals 61 ms, while a response timeout alone cannot establish whether commit occurred; reconcile the order identifier in the application ledger.
cases.check: 6+11+14+27+3=61 ms; removing the 14-ms TLS stage yields 47 ms only in the hypothetical trace, not measured performance.
cases.counter: Treating a lost HTTP response as a rolled-back database transaction is false; the transport and persistence boundaries are independent.
cases.vary: Add 4 ms to DNS (10 ms) and predict 65 ms total with the same application result.
cases.limit: RFC 9110 specifies protocol semantics, not the ordering or latency of a particular application stack.

cases.q: If an application offers Idempotency-Key for creating invoices, what may a caller infer after replaying the same key, and what remains unproven?
cases.setup: Illustrative server contract deduplicates accepted POSTs by the key; requests carry keys [K7,K7]. This is a local contract, not automatic HTTP POST behavior.
cases.derive: There is one distinct accepted key, so one invoice is created under the stated application contract.
cases.check: Count the distinct nonempty keys, |{K7}|=1; replacing replay with a new key K8 yields two invoices.
cases.counter: HTTP POST is not inherently idempotent, and the presence of a header by itself does not prove the server implements replay storage or payload-match checking.
cases.vary: Send [K7,K8] and predict two distinct accepted invoices; verify a reused key with different payload would require a documented conflict rule.
cases.limit: RFC 9110 defines method idempotency; the deduplication model is an illustrative application-specific extension.

cases.q: Why does a 205-ms browser waterfall not establish that a backend spent 205 ms executing code?
cases.setup: Synthetic non-overlapping phases: DNS 12, connection 28, TLS 43, wait-for-first-byte 105 and receive 17 ms.
cases.derive: 12+28+43+105+17=205 ms end-to-end; only a subset of 105-ms waiting time may represent server compute.
cases.check: Break out phases and recompute 205; if first-byte wait rises to 145 ms, end-to-end sum becomes 245 ms.
cases.counter: Calling 205 ms 'database query time' is unsupported because network, queuing and application stages are not isolated.
cases.vary: Raise only first-byte wait by 40 ms and ask which instrument (server trace/span) is needed to localize the added delay.
cases.limit: HTTP semantics alone do not define DevTools phase labels or actual overlap; these are invented strictly additive observations.

cases.q: How do status-code families classify 201, 304, 429, and 503 without equating them to application success?
cases.setup: Four invented responses [201,304,429,503] are observed; classification uses hundreds digit.
cases.derive: 201→2xx; 304→3xx; 429→4xx; 503→5xx. A 304 is conditional response metadata, not an ordinary 200 body.
cases.check: Integer division by 100 yields [2,3,4,5]; [101,206,308,418] yields [1,2,3,4].
cases.counter: 'All 3xx replies redirect to a Location URL' fails for 304 Not Modified.
cases.vary: Replace input with 101,206,308,418 and explain why classifications do not determine whether an application's operation completed.
cases.limit: RFC 9110 defines status semantics; a class digit alone cannot certify business-layer correctness.

cases.q: When identical PUT requests arrive twice, why is a stable resource representation compatible with two audit events?
cases.setup: An illustrative resource begins with {a:1,b:2}; PUT requests both specify complete desired replacement {a:3}.
cases.derive: After both replacements, representation is {a:3}; omitted b is not retained by this full-replacement application model.
cases.check: Apply the same replacement twice; state remains {a:3}. With complete replacement {a:3,b:2}, b is present by explicit request.
cases.counter: Idempotency does not require identical response status codes, zero request logging, or exactly-once delivery.
cases.vary: Change replacement body to include b and contrast final state rather than audit count.
cases.limit: Actual PUT implementation and metadata rules depend on origin semantics; this fixture models only complete replacement state.

cases.q: Can GET and HEAD be classified as safe while POST and PUT cannot, even when all four are authenticated?
cases.setup: Classify intended user-requested action of methods [GET,HEAD,POST,PUT], not incidental server logging.
cases.derive: RFC 9110 marks GET and HEAD safe, whereas POST and PUT permit requested state change; booleans [true,true,false,false].
cases.check: Compare OPTIONS and TRACE, which are also specified as safe methods, noting servers may disable TRACE.
cases.counter: Safe means the client did not request a state-changing effect, not that zero bytes or logs could change at the server.
cases.vary: Classify [OPTIONS,TRACE,DELETE] to obtain [true,true,false] and distinguish safety from permissibility.
cases.limit: Method classifications specify intended semantics; an implementation violating them remains possible and unsafe.

cases.q: When an ETag matches If-None-Match on a conditional GET, why does the origin choose 304 rather than return the body?
cases.setup: Synthetic selected representation has ETag "rev7", request If-None-Match "rev7"; assume method GET and otherwise eligible 200.
cases.derive: With the selected representation unchanged and validator matching, GET precondition yields 304 Not Modified.
cases.check: Switch supplied validator to "rev6" and expect the ordinary 200 selected representation response.
cases.counter: 304 is not a guarantee that local client content exists; a client missing cached representation cannot construct the body from 304 alone.
cases.vary: Replace only request validator; explain how a stale cache reuses an existing stored representation upon successful validation.
cases.limit: Precondition evaluation may interact with additional request fields and selected-resource state beyond this single-ETag model.

cases.q: Why does PUT of a single-field document not mean 'patch that field' under full replacement semantics?
cases.setup: The illustrative target has fields [x=1,y=2]; complete PUT representation contains [x=4] only.
cases.derive: Replacement produces [x=4], with y absent; HTTP PATCH, not PUT, is the conventional method for a partial update contract.
cases.check: Reapply [x=4] and obtain the same one-field representation; include y=5 explicitly and final representation has two fields.
cases.counter: Assuming a PUT body merges silently with unmentioned fields masks destructive client/server contract mismatches.
cases.vary: Send complete replacement [x=4,y=5] and identify exactly which fields survive.
cases.limit: How an origin maps representation to storage is implementation-specific; this exercise explicitly assumes full replacement.

cases.q: Can a DELETE be idempotent if first call returns 204 and retry returns 404?
cases.setup: Illustrative API chooses 204 on deleting an existing resource and 404 when the same resource is already absent; initial resource exists.
cases.derive: Sequence [204,404] leaves resource absent after either request, so user-requested final effect is stable.
cases.check: Starting from already absent yields [404,404] under this particular response policy.
cases.counter: Requiring equal response codes across retries confuses method idempotency with identical message bytes.
cases.vary: Start absent, then issue identical requests; compare both replies and terminal resource state.
cases.limit: RFC 9110 permits different responses on repeated DELETE; exact status policy is a documented choice of this mock origin.

cases.q: What diagnostic information is lost when a monitor reduces 103,206,302,404,503 to only 'pass/fail'?
cases.setup: Synthetic monitor observes [103,206,302,404,503], including informational, partial, redirect, client and server status classes.
cases.derive: Families are [1,2,3,4,5]; 206 is successful partial representation, while 503 signals temporary unavailability in common cases.
cases.check: Change input to [200,201,204,304,429], then recompute [2,2,2,3,4].
cases.counter: Treating 206 as a whole-object download or treating 304 as a redirect to a different URL are incorrect.
cases.vary: Ask which response needs an accompanying Content-Range header and which a cached representation for useful processing.
cases.limit: A status class is a protocol observation; it cannot establish SLA or application correctness without a contract.

cases.q: For a cacheable response with max-age=120 seconds, is Age=80 fresh and Age=120 fresh?
cases.setup: Assume RFC 9111 age calculation already resulted in 80 s and explicit freshness lifetime is 120 s, with no overriding directives.
cases.derive: 80 < 120 means fresh; at boundary 120 < 120 is false, so stale.
cases.check: Compute remaining freshness 120−80=40 s; at Age=120, remaining lifetime is zero.
cases.counter: A stored entry having a 200 status code does not by itself make it fresh or authorize reuse without validation.
cases.vary: Increase Age to exactly 120 s and require revalidation or allowed stale-serving exception.
cases.limit: Corrected initial age, date skew, validators and request directives can change a real cache decision; this is an isolated comparison.

cases.q: What does a HEAD response tell you about a 1,024-byte representation while carrying zero response-content bytes?
cases.setup: Illustrative handler knows a selected GET representation encoded as 1,024 octets and issues equivalent HEAD without content.
cases.derive: Modeled HEAD body is 0 bytes; Content-Length, if sent correctly, describes the corresponding content size 1,024, not zero.
cases.check: Change request to GET under same representation and modeled content body is 1,024 bytes.
cases.counter: Declaring Content-Length: 0 just because HEAD carries no response content confuses metadata for selected representation with transfer payload.
cases.vary: Compare HEAD and GET body length while holding selected representation constant.
cases.limit: A server may omit some header fields for HEAD; byte-exact equality of all GET/HEAD headers is not guaranteed.

cases.q: Does a GET that increments internal request logs cease being safe when no requested account balance changes?
cases.setup: Model GET with 3 incidental audit records and zero user-requested resource writes.
cases.derive: Safety concerns the requested effect: zero requested writes means the modeled GET is safe even if three logs exist.
cases.check: Keep audit count fixed at three but introduce one requested balance mutation; the resulting endpoint violates safe GET intent.
cases.counter: Safety does not mean absolutely no side effects; incidental accounting/advertising/log activity may occur.
cases.vary: Redesign an endpoint that debits on GET to use an unsafe method and appropriate authorization.
cases.limit: The test evaluates stated requested effects, not a production origin's actual behavior.

cases.q: Why is a crawler's GET /cancel?job=42 dangerous if the endpoint cancels the job?
cases.setup: Assume automated prefetch performs GET; in unsafe implementation handler cancels queued job.
cases.derive: A safe method must not request cancellation. In the corrected fixture mutation=false, so crawler GET has no requested state change.
cases.check: Change mutation flag true and the model rejects safe-method contract, regardless of HTTP 200 reply.
cases.counter: Hiding an unsafe verb in the query string does not change the semantics of GET to an unsafe operation.
cases.vary: Move cancellation to an authenticated POST and compare the prefetch consequences.
cases.limit: This is a synthetic contract check; no real endpoints were contacted.

cases.q: A PUT response is lost after persisting {mode:'standby'}. Why can an identical retry be safe with respect to intended final state?
cases.setup: Simulated state machine sets complete resource to mode='standby' twice in series.
cases.derive: Both writes produce one final representation {mode:'standby'}; no requirement that log rows or total requests equal one.
cases.check: Replace second payload with mode='active' and final state becomes {mode:'active'}, proving only identical repeats are covered.
cases.counter: Concluding 'the first request definitely failed' from a missing response can lead to invalid exactly-once claims.
cases.vary: Replay the identical request three times; separately inspect an audit counter without treating it as intended resource state.
cases.limit: Idempotent semantics do not establish end-to-end exactly-once execution of external business side effects.

cases.q: How many distinct terminal resource states result from one versus three identical DELETE attempts?
cases.setup: Mock state initially exists; calls delete the same URI once or three times, ignoring varying response metadata.
cases.derive: After any positive number of deletes, exists=false. This final-state identity, not response equality, is the idempotent property.
cases.check: One call and three calls both yield false; zero calls would leave the initial true state unchanged.
cases.counter: An audit log recording three attempts is not evidence that the resource has been deleted three separate times.
cases.vary: Contrast one attempt with zero; this identifies the required precondition that at least one request reached the handler.
cases.limit: The model excludes concurrent recreation; DELETE idempotency does not freeze a resource against other actors.

cases.q: What is the result of conditional GET with a nonmatching validator, and what cannot be inferred from it?
cases.setup: Server selects ETag "v2"; client sends If-None-Match "v1". Assume no other preconditions and representation otherwise eligible.
cases.derive: ETag mismatch causes normal 200 representation response in this synthetic case, not 304.
cases.check: Replace the client validator with "v2" and conditional GET returns 304, allowing a stored representation to be reused.
cases.counter: A mismatch does not prove resource is entirely new; a minor version update is sufficient.
cases.vary: Change only the validator and re-evaluate; do not assume a 304 response includes representation bytes.
cases.limit: Weak comparison rules and additional validators are omitted; do not generalize this exact-match model to all ETag syntax.

cases.q: For a 1,000-byte resource, how many representation bytes does Range: bytes=100-199 select?
cases.setup: Assume stable 1,000-octet selected representation and one satisfiable inclusive byte range 100 through 199.
cases.derive: Inclusive length =199−100+1=100 bytes; status is 206 with Content-Range: bytes 100-199/1000 in a compliant single-range response.
cases.check: Changing end to 249 yields 249−100+1=150 bytes and a correspondingly different Content-Range.
cases.counter: Off-by-one 199−100=99 discards an endpoint; a 206 response is not equivalent to a complete 200 object.
cases.vary: Alter end offset and verify selected slice length plus Content-Range; separately test unsatisfiable start≥1000 (416).
cases.limit: This numeric model does not cover multipart ranges, If-Range, or servers that ignore Range and return 200.

cases.q: When a selected representation has 256 decoded bytes but 64 encoded bytes, which length belongs in HEAD Content-Length?
cases.setup: Assume GET would transmit a 64-octet content-coded representation selected by negotiation, while its decoded size is 256.
cases.derive: A correct modeled HEAD that includes Content-Length advertises 64 content octets of the corresponding coded GET response, and transfers none.
cases.check: Compare modeled GET for same content coding: 64 transferred octets; 256 is the decoded application payload size.
cases.counter: Publishing the uncompressed size 256 as Content-Length when the selected content-coding emits 64 octets misrepresents the selected transfer content.
cases.vary: Change request to GET without altering Accept-Encoding; validate body sizes for matching selection.
cases.limit: Actual framing, transformations and header elision differ; this exercise explicitly fixes the selected representation and coding.

cases.q: Can HEAD with If-None-Match produce 304 while never supplying the requested representation body?
cases.setup: Selected ETag is "e4", request conditional HEAD validator "e4". Assume selection otherwise 200.
cases.derive: Matching validator yields 304 in this illustrative server; response-content size is zero whether 304 or a normal 200 HEAD.
cases.check: Change validator to "e3": status 200 for HEAD, still zero content bytes; status and content length are separate dimensions.
cases.counter: Assuming 304 includes a body, or that an ordinary 200 HEAD contains GET content, violates their semantics.
cases.vary: Change only validator and preserve zero transfer-content rule under HEAD.
cases.limit: Actual conditional request evaluation may have different precedence under additional headers; only isolated ETag equality is modeled.

cases.q: Two identical POST /orders requests occur after a lost response. Without a documented idempotency contract, how many creations may happen?
cases.setup: Application creation model accepts two POSTs without keys, assigning distinct order IDs; model intentionally does not assume deduplication.
cases.derive: Two accepted POST requests can create two orders; the server cannot infer replay from coincidentally equal payloads by HTTP semantics alone.
cases.check: Introduce an application-defined identical key K9 on both and a verified key store; this illustrative system then produces one order.
cases.counter: Assuming POST is idempotent because request bodies are equal may double-bill after transport retries.
cases.vary: Send two copies under same application key, then vary the body under that key and require contract-specific conflict handling.
cases.limit: HTTP defines POST as generally non-idempotent; behavior of any Idempotency-Key protocol must be explicitly implemented and tested.

cases.q: Why is 422 a valid application response to syntactically valid JSON with an invalid negative quantity?
cases.setup: Fictional order endpoint has schema amount>0 and responds 201 if amount accepted, 422 otherwise; JSON syntax is valid in both branches.
cases.derive: Amount −2 fails domain rule and yields 422 Unprocessable Content under this chosen contract, whereas +2 creates a resource and yields 201.
cases.check: Perturb only sign, from −2 to 2; explain this tests domain validation, not HTTP transport or JSON parser reliability.
cases.counter: Treating every HTTP 4xx response as a network failure confuses application validation with connection health.
cases.vary: Add separate deliberately malformed JSON test, which requires 400 under this fictional contract rather than 422.
cases.limit: RFC 9110 defines 422 semantics; exact validation status mapping is origin-specific and not mandated for all negative values.

cases.q: If a request fails authentication and also has an invalid payload, which stage's status should be diagnosed first?
cases.setup: Fictional gateway checks authentication before request-body validation: authenticated=false, payloadValid=false.
cases.derive: The gateway returns 401 before it validates the body. With authentication corrected but body unchanged, handler returns synthetic 422.
cases.check: Change only authenticated to true and observe 422; proof of authentication failure did not imply payload validity.
cases.counter: Concluding 'the payload must be valid' because the first response was 401 ignores validation short-circuiting.
cases.vary: Test authenticated=true, payloadValid=true and record 200 by this endpoint's example routing.
cases.limit: Ordering and mapping are example application policy, not globally enforced by HTTP RFC 9110.

cases.q: With max-age=300, s-maxage=60 and Age=120, why is a shared cache stale while a private cache is fresh?
cases.setup: Cacheable synthetic response age is 120 seconds, max-age=300, s-maxage=60; no restrictive overriding directives.
cases.derive: Shared cache uses s-maxage=60: 120<60 false (stale). Private cache uses max-age=300: 120<300 true (fresh).
cases.check: Compute remaining shared lifetime −60 s and private +180 s, then compare same response under both cache roles.
cases.counter: Applying max-age=300 to shared cache while ignoring s-maxage violates explicit directive precedence.
cases.vary: Switch only cache role shared→private and predict freshness flips while Age and response headers remain fixed.
cases.limit: Corrected Age, authentication restrictions, Vary, request directives, and stale-serving exceptions are excluded from the isolated example.
